summary: Updates the recommended list of key exchange methods for the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol so they meet stronger security expectations. Key exchange is the step where client and server agree on a secret for the session. The document revises earlier SSH RFCs to say which methods should be used and which should be avoided.

plainLanguage.summary: When two people want a secret handshake, they must first agree how to invent it safely. This note updates the list of safe ways to do that for remote logins.

subtitle: Which SSH key exchange methods to require, encourage, discourage or ban, now that SHA-1 and small keys are no longer strong enough.

tldr.problem: The key exchange methods that SSH originally required, built on SHA-1 and small 1024-bit parameters, are no longer considered secure enough.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC changes the requirement level of each published SSH key exchange method name, using 112 bits of security strength as the minimum, and records the result in one summary table and in the IANA registry.
tldr.outcome: diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 becomes the one MUST, curve25519-sha256 is a SHOULD, and SHA-1 based methods and rsa1024-sha1 are pushed out.

today: RFC 9142 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2022. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 4250, RFC 4253, RFC 4432 and RFC 4462.

sections.title: Why the List Needed Updating
sections.content:
In RFC 4253, SSH defined two key exchange (KEX) method names that MUST be implemented. Over time, what was once considered secure no longer is. This RFC recommends that some published key exchanges be deprecated or disallowed, that some SHOULD be adopted, and that one MUST be adopted.

It updates RFC 4250, RFC 4253, RFC 4432 and RFC 4462 by moving the requirement level of various methods: a MUST moving to SHOULD, MAY or SHOULD NOT, and a MAY moving to MUST, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT or MUST NOT.

The key exchange produces a shared secret K and an exchange hash H. Encryption and authentication keys are derived from these, and H from the first exchange also becomes the session identifier. Both the strength of the public key algorithm and the hash used in the key derivation function (KDF) affect how secure K is.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook for making a secret handshake has some rules that are now too easy to guess. This note fixes the rulebook.

sections.title: Choosing Hashes and Strength Levels
sections.content:
SHA-1 has been attacked and is no longer strong enough for SSH. It provides approximately 80 bits of security strength. For key exchange, the relevant attacks are chosen-prefix collisions. The RFC cites transcript collision attacks, which could tamper with the exchanged algorithm lists and possibly downgrade the negotiated ciphersuite. These attacks remain computationally very difficult, but any key exchange using SHA-1 should be phased out as soon as possible, and if it is kept for compatibility it should be listed last in the preference list.

The SHA-2 family is strongly advised. SHA2-256 has 128 bits of security strength, SHA2-384 has 192 and SHA2-512 has 256. The suggested minimum hash for key exchange is SHA2-256. The document sets 112 bits of security strength as its minimum, matching the weakest listed symmetric cipher, 3des-cbc. It also advises matching the strength of the key exchange with that of the cipher, since attackers can target the weakest element of the handshake.
sections.plainLanguage: A lock is only as good as its weakest part. The note says to throw out the old flimsy hash and always use one at least as strong as the rest of the setup.

sections.title: Three Families of Key Exchange
sections.content:
SSH uses three kinds of mathematically hard problems for key exchange.

  • Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC): NIST prime curves and others via ECDH (RFC 5656), and curve25519 and curve448 (RFC 8731). Across the named curves the minimum strength is approximately 128 bits; the RFC lists nistp256 at 128, nistp384 at 192, nistp521 at 512, curve25519 at 128 and curve448 at 224 bits.
  • Finite Field Cryptography (FFC): Diffie-Hellman with safe primes from a fixed list (RFC 3526) or generated dynamically (RFC 4419, updated by RFC 8270). A modulus of at least 2048 bits gives about 112 bits of strength.
  • Integer Factorization Cryptography (IFC): RSA key exchange from RFC 4432. RSA 1024-bit keys give about 80 bits and RSA 2048-bit keys about 112 bits. IFC key exchanges do not provide Forward Secrecy, which FFC and ECC both do.

Larger groups, curves or keys cost more computation.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three different kinds of puzzles two computers can use to agree on a secret. Bigger puzzles are safer but slower to solve.

sections.title: The New Requirement Levels
sections.content:
Weak methods are moved to deprecated (SHOULD NOT) or disallowed (MUST NOT). Newer or stronger methods that need more resources are allowed (MAY). Methods with implementation consensus that are not weak are encouraged (SHOULD). At least one method must be promoted to mandatory to implement (MTI). Any method not explicitly listed MAY be implemented.

  • MUST: diffie-hellman-group14-sha256, a simple step from the older group14-sha1 since only the hash changes.
  • SHOULD: curve25519-sha256, diffie-hellman-group16-sha512, the three ecdh-sha2-nistp* curves, and the GSS-API counterparts of several of these.
  • MAY: curve448-sha512, diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256, groups 15, 17 and 18, rsa2048-sha256, ecmqv-sha2, and diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 (put at the end of the list).
  • SHOULD NOT: diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 and diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1.
  • MUST NOT: rsa1024-sha1.

MODP groups with a modulus under 2048 bits are weak and MUST NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The note sorts the methods into 'you have to know this one', 'please learn these', 'optional', 'try not to use' and 'never use'.

sections.title: Why group14-sha1 Is Still Tolerated
sections.content:
Before this document, diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 and diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 were both MTI. Group1 is a 1024-bit MODP group with approximately 80 bits of security, which is too weak to keep. Group14 is a 2048-bit group.

Many implementers asked that group14-sha1 be deprecated first and only disallowed later, rather than jump straight from MTI to disallowed. The RFC mentions small Internet of Things devices that lack the compute and memory to use larger groups before a session times out. There was consensus to keep it as a MAY for interoperability with legacy implementations, at the end of the negotiated list, with the expectation it will be deprecated or disallowed later.

The document also says that all key exchange methods using SHA-1 should be deprecated and phased out, and that there is currently no SSH key exchange using the SHA-3 family. The extension negotiation indicators ext-info-c and ext-info-s from RFC 8308 SHOULD both be implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: An old key is being retired slowly, because some tiny gadgets cannot yet use the newer, bigger one. It goes to the back of the line first.

sections.title: The Summary Table
sections.content:
Section 4 lists every known key exchange method name alphabetically with its reference, its previous recommendation and the new one from this RFC. Some changes are large. For example diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 goes from MUST to MAY, diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 from MUST to SHOULD NOT, rsa1024-sha1 from MAY to MUST NOT, and each ecdh-sha2-nistp* curve from MUST to SHOULD.

The full set of official IANA key exchange method names not otherwise mentioned MAY be implemented.

IANA added an "OK to Implement" column to the "Key Exchange Method Names" registry. Entries marked MUST NOT are considered disallowed; entries marked SHOULD NOT are deprecated and may be disallowed in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one big chart showing what each method was before and what it is now.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SSH provides a secure encrypted channel over an insecure network, performing server host authentication, key exchange, encryption and integrity checks. The full security considerations in RFC 4251 and those in RFC 4432 continue to apply. Forward Secrecy is NOT available with rsa1024-sha1 or rsa2048-sha256.

The goal is to deprecate or disallow weak methods before they are broken while still in use. A method is weak when its strength is insufficient for the symmetric cipher or the algorithm has been broken. The 1024-bit MODP group of group1-sha1, any MODP group under 2048 bits, and rsa1024-sha1 are called too small. SHA-1 may not be completely broken, but the RFC says it is time to retire all uses as soon as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: If a lock is going to be picked eventually, better to change it before burglars learn how.
